# vendor

gpui-kit's code editor, forked so it can be made fast enough for large files (measured by `koyo-rs/koyo-bench`).

| Directory | Crate | Version | Upstream |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gpui-base/` | `gpui-base` | 0.10.0 | [longbridge/gpui-kit](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit) `crates/base` at `f697c3133d55c64fa8a5b67926147fb3dadd276d` |
| `gpui-component/` | `gpui-component` | 0.10.0 | [longbridge/gpui-kit](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit) `crates/component` at the same commit |
| `gpui-fast-apple/` | `gpui-fast-apple` | 0.1.17 | the crates.io package, unpacked from the `.crate` whose checksum crates.io publishes for that version (the package names no commit) |
| `gpui-fast-macos/` | `gpui-fast-macos` | 0.1.17 | the crates.io package ([longbridge/gpui-fast](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-fast)), unpacked the same way |

Both started as the crates.io packages unpacked as they are, `Cargo.toml` (as normalized by crates.io), `Cargo.toml.orig`, `Cargo.lock`, `.cargo_vcs_info.json` and `LICENSE-APACHE` included; each `.crate` matched the checksum in the workspace's `Cargo.lock` before it was unpacked. `git log -- koyo-rs/vendor/` shows what has changed since.

An update to newer packages is a three-way merge of every file: the base is the published file of the version vendored until then, ours the file here, theirs the new published file, each `.crate` checked against the checksum crates.io publishes for its version (`https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/<name>/<version>`). A file only upstream added or removed follows upstream, so each folder is the new package as unpacked plus the changes described here, but for what [the last update left out](#what-the-update-to-0100-and-0117-left-out).

The workspace's `Cargo.toml` (`koyo-rs/Cargo.toml`) puts them in place of the registry crates with `[patch.crates-io]`. The `gpui-kit` facade still comes from crates.io and re-exports both, so the build holds one copy of each: `cargo tree -i gpui-base` names `vendor/gpui-base`.

Neither crate is a workspace member. They keep upstream's code style and their own `[lints]` table; the workspace lint policy and `script/hygiene` cover the `koyo-rs/koyo*` crates only. Being path dependencies, their warnings aren't capped as a registry crate's are: `script/lint` holds them to rustc's and Clippy's defaults with every warning an error.

All four are licensed Apache-2.0, as is this repository; their license files (`LICENSE-APACHE`, `LICENSE`) stay with them.

## gpui-fast-apple

GPUI's Metal renderer, vendored for three changes, marked `Koyo:` in `src/metal_renderer.rs`, `src/shaders.metal`, `src/fast/rounded_clip_shader.rs` and `src/fast/composition.rs`. The first: it draws a BGRA surface in the window's own frame: a simulator's or the agent desktop's picture, in the surface its host shares with the app (`koyo-rs/koyo/src/surfaces.rs`). A browser page's frame came the same way until pages became native views (`docs/native-pages.md`); what was only a page's, a picture smaller than its surface (`set_surface_picture`), has no caller now and is still in the renderer. Upstream draws only biplanar video surfaces. The renderer speaks to Metal through `objc2-metal`, as upstream's has since 0.1.17; the features of it these changes need (`objc2-io-surface` among them) are in the normalized `Cargo.toml`. `metal_renderer::set_surface_picture` says how much of the shared surface, from its top left, is the page; that part goes over the surface's bounds, and the rest of its content mask is filled by the picture's edge pixels reaching out, as while a page is laid out a frame behind a pane that grew. Rounded clips apply to it as to GPUI's other primitives. A page surface's Metal texture is made over its `IOSurface` directly, not through Core Video's texture cache, which keeps a pixel buffer until the cache is flushed; each frame keeps the pixel buffers and textures of the page surfaces it samples until the GPU has finished it (a pixel buffer marks its surface in use while it lives, which the browser host reads before painting into a surface), and no longer. Drawn with everything round it, the page can't reach the screen a frame apart from the pane's edge, which a page in a layer of its own did unless GPUI presented in Core Animation's transaction, at the cost of the window's frame rate. `build.rs` also allows the unused `stage` its shader helper module has when shaders aren't compiled ahead of time, as a path dependency's warnings aren't capped.

The second: it takes a picture of part of a frame, for the tab switcher's cards (`koyo-rs/koyo/src/shell/pictures.rs`, `docs/tab-switcher.md` 4). `metal_renderer::set_surface_capture` marks a BGRA pixel buffer as one a picture is taken into. Painted in a scene, such a buffer draws nothing; once the frame is drawn, `MetalRenderer::take_pictures` copies the frame's pixels under the buffer's bounds, as far as its content mask shows them, into a texture with mips, and draws that, shrunk, into the buffer's own `IOSurface` with the page surfaces' pipeline, whose sampler reads the mips for it (`shaders.metal`). Another buffer over the same surface then paints as any BGRA surface. A picture is taken at most every quarter second while the buffer's request stays the same, and with the next frame when it changes. Only a surface painted in the frame's own scene has its picture taken, not one inside a layer's content. A window's frames can't be read while its layer is display-only (`framebufferOnly`), which upstream leaves it outside debug builds with `test-support`: the first picture asked of a window turns that off for each of its layers, and is taken from the next frame.

A window that composes native views draws in layers, each a frame of its own with a renderer of its own (`src/fast/composition.rs`), and a picture is of all of them. The lowest layer's renderer takes it as above; the renderer of a layer over it (`MetalRenderer::draws_over`) then draws its own part of the frame over that picture, once for each the lowest takes. The layers' renderers share what they keep of the window's pictures, the last one taken and the texture a part of a frame is copied into, and one command queue, which upstream now gives every renderer on a device anyway, so the GPU draws the upper part after the lower. The native views themselves are in no frame: `metal_renderer::set_surface_pane` marks a BGRA buffer as a pane, which draws nothing in a scene and which the renderer of an upper layer fills in a picture, rounded, under its own part. Koyo's native surfaces can paint one over themselves, as its Liquid Glass does (`koyo-rs/koyo/src/native/surface.rs`). One attachment says what a surface is, a page's picture, one a picture is taken into or a pane (`Mark`), so drawing a surface reads it once.

The third: it draws a chat's backdrop, a texture Koyo made itself, which no pixel buffer can hold: the screen's picture compressed to ASTC (`koyo-rs/koyo/src/chat_backdrop/`, `docs/chat-backdrop.md` 4). `metal_renderer::register_texture` makes a texture of ASTC blocks, 4 × 4 or 8 × 8, on the system's GPU, from any thread, and gives it a number; its colours are read as they are (`ASTC_*_LDR`), as the atlas's BGRA is, not taken out of sRGB. `set_surface_backdrop` marks a BGRA pixel buffer, a pixel of it, as standing for that number and saying how it looks (`Mark::Backdrop`). Painted, the whole texture goes over the surface's bounds, as far as its content mask shows them, its rounded clips with it, drawn by a shader of its own (`backdrop_vertex`, `backdrop_fragment` in `shaders.metal`): in cells of a few pixels from the bounds' top left, each sampled at its middle and lit or not by a 4 × 4 Bayer matrix, a lit cell at its colour's full brightness and an unlit one at 8 % of it, at an opacity, fading out down the content mask. The look is Monodrive's Dither effect ([donnes/monodrive](https://github.com/donnes/monodrive), MIT, © 2026 Donald Silveira), which dithers on the CPU and fades in a pass of its own; no code of it is copied. The command buffer keeps the texture while the GPU reads it, and `release_texture` lets it go.

## gpui-fast-macos

GPUI's macOS windows, vendored for changes marked `Koyo:` in `src/fast/composition.rs`, `src/window.rs` and `src/responders.rs`, each but the blur's for a window that composes native views (`docs/native-pages.md` 6):

- Whose a mouse button's events are (`send_window_event`). Upstream at 0.1.12 gave each drag move to whatever lay under the pointer, and kept one native view as the owner of every button until it had counted each button's release. A drag pressed on GPUI's own content, a divider beside a browser page, lost the moves made over the page; and a release the window never saw (a menu the press opened had tracked it, a drag session had taken it) left that view the owner for good, every later drag of any button going to it. Here a press owns its button: the view that took a button's press, by the button's number, gets that button's drag and release wherever the pointer is by then, a button whose press GPUI took has no entry and its events go GPUI's way, each press says anew whose its button is, and a view that leaves the window holds no press. Upstream at 0.1.17 has an answer of its own (`PointerCapture`): still one owner for every button down, GPUI or a native view, let go when a tracked button is pressed again, and GPUI's drags and releases handed to its view without `AppKit`. This crate keeps its own and leaves that out. Of upstream's it has two things: a press on the window's own chrome, its resize border or titlebar buttons, goes to `AppKit` and is nobody's, told to the app as a press on GPUI's content (`hits_window_chrome`); and where upstream lets go of its owner, as the window stops being active, starts being moved or starts a drag session, every press here is let go (`clear_pointer_capture`).
- A release GPUI never hears (`lost_releases`). GPUI's core holds a press over a native view as that view's until it hears the release, and meanwhile no press reaches GPUI's own content. GPUI's view keeps the presses it passed on and, once a move with no button down or a press while the hand's button for one is up says a press is over, tells GPUI of its release first.
- The modifiers (`send_window_event`, `route_keys`). A flags-changed event goes to GPUI's view as well whenever another view, a page's, has the keyboard: GPUI hears the modifiers only through its own view, and ⌃ let go after ⌃⇥ in a page never reached the tab switcher. GPUI already counts a change it hears twice once.
- The app's say over the keyboard (`src/responders.rs`, `docs/keyboard.md`). The app gives the windows a `Responders` (`set_responders`), which each of GPUI's windows and panels tells, on the main thread: every change of its first responder, whoever made it (`makeFirstResponder:`, overridden on both window classes, calls `AppKit`'s own and then tells the change); every key going down or up before the window delivers it to its first responder (`route_keys`, in `send_window_event`: key equivalents have been offered by then, by the application, and aren't touched); and every press of a mouse button before it's handed on, with the view under the pointer when it's in a native view of the composition (from the hit test `send_window_event` makes anyway) or nil for GPUI's own content (`tell_press`). Upstream has none of it: a native view that took the first responder on its own, as a browser page does as it opens, kept every key with GPUI never hearing of it. With no `Responders` given, the windows behave as upstream's, but for the other changes here.
- A key offered to GPUI's view while another view has the keyboard is the app's to route (`src/responders.rs`, `Responders::key_route`; `handle_key_event`; `koyoHandBackKey:`; `gpui_hears_up`). `AppKit` offers every ⌘ and ⌃ key and every function key, the arrows among them, to the window's views as a key equivalent before it delivers the key, and upstream runs everything on a key so offered, the text system too, which types into whatever has the keyboard: a left arrow in a browser page's field put a control character there and, answered as taken, never reached the page. GPUI's view now says who offers the key (`AppKit`'s pass, or the view that had the keyboard handing it back, which has a selector of its own, `koyoHandBackKey:`) and what has the keyboard, and does what the app answers: everything, its bindings alone, or nothing. The rule is the app's (`koyo-seam`, `keys::route`). A key handed back whose bindings GPUI ran has its going up told to GPUI's view too. `handle_key_event` is a function of Rust's own for it, no longer `extern "C"`. With no `Responders` given, a key is handled as upstream.
- A press that goes on to a native view is told (`src/responders.rs`, `Responders::delivered`; `send_window_event`). `pressed` tells a press before GPUI has had its say over it; `delivered` tells, with the view the press was hit-tested to, that GPUI didn't keep it and the native view is about to hear it. The app gives a browser page the keyboard by it (`docs/keyboard.md` 5): a page's view doesn't always ask for the first responder after a press.
- The native views put back is told (`src/responders.rs`, `Responders::remounted`; `set_composition_order`; `MacWindow::set_composition_order`). When the order or the tree of a window's surfaces changes, upstream takes every native view out of the window and puts it back, and a view that had the first responder loses it to the window, which `AppKit` does without asking. The window notes that it did, and tells the app once it has let go of its state; the app puts the first responder back on the next turn.
- A made-up release is logged (`lost_releases`): one line at `koyo::input` for each release GPUI is told of that it never heard, naming the button only.
- How strongly a blurred window blurs (`setKoyoBlurScale:` on `BlurredView`, `scale_blur`). The app scales the radius of the Gaussian blur filter `NSVisualEffectView` gives its backdrop layer, which has no public setting: `blurred_view_update_layer` sets it again after each of `AppKit`'s updates, as it already strips the material's tint and saturation, from the radius the material first had, kept on the view. Upstream leaves the material's radius.
- A key equivalent matched by its event (`handle_key_event`). Upstream lets a key press go by when it's the same keystroke as the last key equivalent, which AppKit sends first for some keys; a key a page leaves comes to GPUI as a key equivalent with no key press after it, and the next same key typed in GPUI was lost. The two are matched by the event's time too.

## What the update to 0.10.0 and 0.1.17 left out

Upstream's code these crates don't take, each because a change described above already does its work another way:

- `gpui-base`: the reuse of a line's wrapping across widths (`src/input/editor/display_map/text_wrapper/measurements.rs` and `wrap_width.rs`, and what `text_wrapper.rs` and `wrap_map.rs` had of them). The editor's lines are wrapped where they are seen and in the background instead (`text_wrapper.rs`, `relayout_wrap` in `src/input/base/state.rs`), and an edit before the first layout still wraps the lines it touches, so upstream's test that it doesn't (`test_set_value_waits_for_the_first_layout`) is left out too. Upstream's other change to that file, a tab's indicator clipped to its tab, is here.
- `gpui-component`: the popovers upstream draws a hover and a diagnostic in (`src/input/popovers/hover_popover.rs`, `diagnostic_popover.rs`) and its placing of a menu over the caret when it doesn't fit under it (`fit_popup_origin` in `caret_anchored.rs`). The editor's cards and its own placing replace them (`cards.rs`, `diagnostic.rs`, `caret_anchored.rs`). Upstream's drawing of these popups at `POPUP_PRIORITY` is here, on the cards too.
- `gpui-fast-macos`: `src/fast/composition_capture.rs`, as the first point under [gpui-fast-macos](#gpui-fast-macos) says.

Two things upstream took over from here, and they are upstream's now: a textarea's decorations (`TextareaState::set_decorations`), which now follow edits and go with a text replaced whole, where they stayed until laid again; and `SelectableText::highlights`, beside which `with_highlights` is kept for the callers that have it.
